language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: JavaScript has strict equality and loose equality, plus relational comparisons that may convert operands.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: === and !== compare without the broad coercions of == and !=. Loose equality follows conversion rules, with null and undefined equal to each other. Relational operators compare numbers or strings after conversions and may invoke object-to-primitive conversion.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: a === b, a !== b, a == b, a != b, a < b, a <= b, Object.is(a,b)
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: Comparison bugs are often hidden because individual test inputs look reasonable while edge inputs cross type boundaries.
common_use: Use strict equality for ordinary application code
Use == null only as deliberate null-or-undefined check
Use relational operators after normalizing input type
common_misuse: Comparing numeric strings to numbers without conversion
Assuming NaN equals itself
Sorting with a comparator that returns booleans instead of negative/zero/positive
debugging_symptoms: Sort order differs by input shape
tests_or_checks: Test numeric strings, empty strings, null, undefined, NaN, objects, and arrays
safe_refactor_notes: When changing == to ===, add tests for the old accepted input types
Normalize at API boundaries before comparison

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: When an object is used where a primitive is expected, JavaScript asks the object for a primitive representation.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: Conversion can use Symbol.toPrimitive, valueOf(), or toString() depending on the operation and hint. The result affects arithmetic, comparison, property keys, string output, and template literals.
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: Custom conversion hooks make ordinary-looking operators run user code and can hide side effects or surprising values.
common_use: Implement domain-specific numeric objects only with care
Debug operator behavior on custom objects
common_misuse: Using objects in comparisons without knowing conversion result
Adding valueOf side effects
Assuming template literal output is diagnostic enough
debugging_symptoms: Map/object keys collapse to same string in plain objects
tests_or_checks: Check for Symbol.toPrimitive, valueOf, toString overrides
Avoid object operands in arithmetic unless designed
safe_refactor_notes: Preserve conversion hooks when moving methods
Prefer explicit method calls for domain values

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: Objects expose values through property names using dot or bracket notation.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: obj.name uses an identifier property name. obj[expr] evaluates expr and converts it to a property key. Accessing a property of null or undefined throws. Lookup may continue through the prototype chain.
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: Most JavaScript objects, arrays, functions, modules, DOM objects, and API results are manipulated through property access.
common_misuse: Reading nested properties before nullish guard
Using dot notation when the key is dynamic
Confusing missing own property with inherited property
tests_or_checks: Test dynamic keys with unusual strings
safe_refactor_notes: When moving properties, preserve accessor/getter semantics and prototype lookup assumptions
Use destructuring only after nullish checks

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: Optional chaining stops a property access or call when the base is nullish and returns undefined instead of throwing.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: ?. applies only at the guarded step. It does not validate later required values unless each access is guarded. It changes failure mode from exception to undefined.
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: Optional chaining is useful at unreliable boundaries but can hide bugs if a value should always exist.
common_use: Handle missing DOM/API elements when absence is valid
common_misuse: Replacing a required invariant with ?. and letting undefined flow downstream
Assuming ?. catches all errors inside a called function
Combining ?. with || defaults that erase valid falsy values
debugging_symptoms: Later NaN or undefined output instead of early TypeError
Tests pass without asserting required structure
tests_or_checks: Ask whether missing base is valid
Test absent intermediate object and present falsy values
safe_refactor_notes: Use explicit assertion for required values

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: Arithmetic operators compute numeric results, while + also concatenates strings.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: Most arithmetic operators convert operands to numbers. + performs string concatenation if either operand is or becomes a string in the relevant conversion path; otherwise it performs numeric addition.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: a + b, a - b, a * b, a / b, a % b, ++x, x++
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: The same plus token is both addition and concatenation, so mixed input types are a common bug source.
common_misuse: Adding form/query values without parsing
Using ++ across line breaks incorrectly
Assuming arrays in arithmetic are invalid before conversion
debugging_symptoms: Counter update uses stale coerced type
tests_or_checks: Test numeric strings and empty strings
safe_refactor_notes: Do not change + to template literal without checking numeric intent

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: Logical operators return operand values, not necessarily booleans, and skip work when the result is already known.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: && returns the first falsy operand or the last operand. || returns the first truthy operand or the last operand. ?? returns the right side only when the left side is null or undefined. ! converts to boolean.
language_semantics_records.syntax_or_api_shape: a && b, a || fallback, a ?? fallback, !a
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: Short-circuit operators are concise control flow and defaulting tools, but they can accidentally treat valid falsy values as missing.
common_misuse: Using || for numeric/string defaults where 0 or "" is valid
Depending on side effects in skipped operands
Assuming result type is boolean
debugging_symptoms: Variable holds object/string instead of boolean
tests_or_checks: Use Boolean(expr) when boolean output is required
safe_refactor_notes: When refactoring to if statements, preserve returned operand value semantics

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: JavaScript can insert semicolons at line breaks, but not at every line break.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: Line terminators may be treated as statement separators when parsing otherwise fails, with important exceptions such as return/throw/yield/break/continue, postfix ++/--, and arrow functions. Lines starting with (, [, /, +, or - can be parsed as continuation of the prior statement.
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: ASI can turn visually reasonable code into different code, especially around return statements and leading parentheses/brackets.
common_use: Omit semicolons consistently with defensive leading semicolons
Use semicolons explicitly to reduce ambiguity
common_misuse: Putting return value on the next line
Starting an IIFE or array literal after a semicolonless statement
Breaking before =>
debugging_symptoms: Previous expression is called as a function
tests_or_checks: Search for return/throw/yield/break/continue followed by newline
Check lines beginning with ( or [ after semicolonless code
safe_refactor_notes: Do not move expressions across line breaks near restricted productions without tests
Prefer explicit semicolons in generated/concatenated snippets

language_semantics_records.plain_language_meaning: Strict mode disables or changes selected legacy JavaScript behaviors.
language_semantics_records.precise_behavior: Strict mode is enabled by a "use strict" directive or implicitly in ES modules and classes. It makes some silent errors throw, changes this in function calls, restricts eval/arguments behavior, and removes certain legacy features.
language_semantics_records.why_it_matters: Strictness affects refactors from scripts to modules/classes and changes behavior of legacy code.
common_misuse: Moving legacy script into module without checking this and globals
Depending on non-strict function-call this
Using restricted identifiers
debugging_symptoms: this is undefined in function call
safe_refactor_notes: Treat script-to-module conversion as behavior change
